newsitem.title: USA: Treasury's Summers--dlr to stay dominant after EMU.
newsitem.headline: Treasury's Summers--dlr to stay dominant after EMU.

text.p: Europe's planned single currency is unlikely to challenge the dollar's position as the world's primary reserve currency in the foreseeable future, Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said on Wednesday.

"I think that the dollar will remain the primary reserve currency for the foreseeable future, and any further erosion in its relative position in the system is likely to happen, if it happens, only slowly," Summers said in a text given to reporters before a speech in New York.
Summers said it is reasonable to expect some prevailing uncertainty over how European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will operate. Credibility typically takes a while to establish, he said.
"It is likely to take some time for the markets to become comfortable with and confident in the new currency," he said.
Europe's major currencies are scheduled to converge into a new unit -- to be called the euro -- in 1999.
The debate over which currencies will meet the tough government deficit and debt criteria to qualify to be the first to join the euro is still underway.

Countries participating in monetary union will give up the capacity to pursue independent exchange rate and monetary policies, Summers said. They will then sacrifice the freedom to pursue domestic policies designed to respond to country-specific economic disturbances, he said.
"In such an environment, EMU makes structural labor market and long-term fiscal reforms even more essential to combating unemployment and achieving robust growth," Summers added.
